newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - British jobless falls to lowest since 1990.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - British jobless falls to lowest since 1990.

text.p: British unemployment fell to its lowest level for almost seven years in April, but the new Labour government immediately announced plans to review the much-criticised figures to make them more credible.

The Office for National Statistics said on Wednesday that unemployment fell by 59,400 to 1.65 million in April, the lowest total since August 1990, giving a jobless rate of 5.9 percent of the workforce.

Underlying average earnings grew by a slower than expected 4.5 percent in the year to March compared with a 5.0 percent rise in the year to February, suggesting a slight easing in inflationary pressures.
The government, which had derided the jobless data as "fantasy figures" while in opposition, welcomed the fall in unemployment but said it was time the figures were overhauled.
This is a bold move as most economists argue that any serious review of the way unemployment is measured will probably show that many more people are out of work.
"Credibility must be restored to the official unemployment statistics. The public have suspected they have been the object of political manipulation," said employment minister Andrew Smith.
The ONS said it would consult economists, statisticians and the media about how best to present the figures and hoped to bring in any changes by the late summer of this year.

Britain is unique in calculating unemployment as the number of people out of work and eligible to claim benefit. Regular changes to the criteria for eligibility have led to major distortions in the data.
Many economists would like Britain to adopt the widely recognised International Labour Organisation measure of unemployment as the number of people out of work and looking for a job.
A recent independent study by Sheffield Hallam University calculated that real unemployment in January was more than double the official 1.8 million figure.
This would represent an unemployment rate of around 13 percent, roughly in line with rates in other key European countries such as Germany and France.
City economists said the move to review the statistics was very welcome and long overdue.
"We have been living with manipulated, distorted data for 15 years," said John Shepperd, chief economist at Yamaichi International.

He said the large number of changes made to the figures over the last 18 years had been tiresome and robbed the series of historical consistency. "But one more change which establishes a sound basis for the figures would be welcome."
Economists agreed that despite flaws in the series, unemployment was clearly falling fast.
While good news on one level, the rapid drop raised fears that companies might have to pay higher wages to secure staff and that this could stoke inflation.
The slower growth in average earnings in March was unlikely to last, economists said.

"With unemployment continuing its rapid decline and the business surveys beginning to show labour shortages...there is good reason to be concerned about the outlook for earnings this year," said James Barty, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Economists noted that 4.5 percent growth in average earnings is still worryingly high as far as the Bank of England, newly empowered to set interest rates, is concerned.

The Bank said on Tuesday that earnings growth much above 4.5 percent would be a worry and warned that interest rates might have to rise soon to choke off inflation. The base lending rate was raised to 6.25 percent from 6.0 percent last week.
